title: A 400lb butcher said he was a dead heir — and his mother believed him. Why?
description:
In 1866, a massively built man arrived in London claiming to be Sir Roger Tichborne, a wealthy heir who had drowned at sea 12 years earlier. He had no tattoo, couldn't speak French, and didn't recognize his own horse — but Roger's grief-stricken mother looked at him once and declared him her son, granting him £1,000 a year.

Lawyers traced him to Arthur Orton, a butcher's son from Wapping. Two of the longest trials in English legal history followed — 103 days, then 188 days. He was convicted of perjury and sentenced to 14 years' hard labor.

He served ten years, sold a confession to a newspaper, recanted it four days later, and died in 1898 still signing letters 'Sir Roger Tichborne.' His coffin plate carried the name he went to prison for stealing.
